events.type: management commentary (CEO TV interview): demand vs supply
events.summary: CEO Michael Hurlston told Bloomberg Television ('The Asia Trade', in Tokyo, aired Thursday evening New York time / Friday morning Tokyo) that Lumentum's optoelectronic parts for AI data centers are 'completely sold out' through almost 2029. Per secondary reports of the interview: it cannot meet about 70% of demand for some products through 2027 and about 30% for others through 2028; laser chips are the tightest constraint; it added a fab in Greensboro, North Carolina and is adding capacity at a second fab in Japan; new laser capacity takes about three years (a year to equip the fab, a year to qualify the device, a year for customers to qualify it). Quote: 'We are really trying to catch up, add capacity as fast as we can, but we are very, very far behind what customers want' (Investopedia). In April 2026 he had told Bloomberg products were sold out through 2027, so the horizon has moved out by more than a year.
events.why_it_matters: It directly supports thesis pillar 2 (demand bigger than supply): a shortage lasting into 2029 usually means pricing power and visible future sales. It also means revenue is capped by how fast Lumentum can add capacity, not by demand. It is a TV interview, not guidance or a filing.

events.summary: Optical stocks fell together from the open: by about noon ET Applied Optoelectronics was -9%, Coherent -5%, Lumentum -4% and the Roundhill photonics fund (LYTE) -6%, with 'no shared headline, no analyst upgrade, and no product news' per 24/7 Wall St, which called it profit-taking after huge gains (Lumentum about +190% this year). No change to Lumentum's own numbers.

why_chain.text: Thursday: Lumentum fell 5.62%. The model splits it into market -0.22, industry (SMH) -4.18 and company -1.22 points (z -0.25, normal size): an industry day.

Thursday: the whole optical group fell from the open with no company news (AAOI -9%, Coherent -5%, LITE -4%, LYTE -6% by noon ET); 24/7 Wall St calls it profit-taking after big gains (LITE about +190% this year).

Thursday morning backdrop: index futures down about 0.5%, oil and Treasury yields rising (inflation worry); one low-tier report adds Fed-minutes rate worries and debate about 1.6T ramps and co-packaged optics replacing pluggable modules.

Thursday afternoon: the FT reported OpenAI told investors its annualized revenue was near $50bn, about $20bn below the roughly $70bn widely reported; AI-exposed chip stocks fell further (Nvidia almost -3%, AMD about -4%, Broadcom about -4.35%). LITE went from -4% at noon to -5.62% at the close.

Thursday basic driver: optics stocks are priced on years of AI data-center spending; a sign that the largest AI buyer earns less than thought raises doubt about how long that spending lasts, and the stocks that rose most (high beta: LITE beta 2.89 vs the market) fall most when risk appetite drops.
Friday: Lumentum rose 5.22% while SMH fell 0.65%; the model puts +7.01 points on the company (z 1.40, within normal noise but clearly company/optics-driven).

Friday: on Thursday evening New York time (after the close), CEO Hurlston told Bloomberg TV in Tokyo that its optoelectronic parts are 'completely sold out' through almost 2029; the stock was up about 3.8% before the open.

Friday: the new information is the length and size of the shortage: about 70% of demand unmet for some products through 2027 and about 30% for others through 2028, versus 'sold out through 2027' in April; new laser capacity (second fab in Japan) takes about three years.

Friday basic driver: when buyers must queue for years, the seller can hold or raise prices and can count on future sales, so investors expect bigger and more certain profits; peers rose too because a sold-out leader implies a tight industry. Part of the gain faded into the close as chip stocks slipped.

products.name: Laser chips for AI optical links (indium phosphide lasers, including ultra-high-power lasers for co-packaged optics)
products.what_it_is: Tiny semiconductor chips that create the laser light that carries data through glass fibre between AI chips and switches.
products.analogy: The bulb in a signalling torch that flashes billions of times a second to send messages down a glass thread.
products.buyers: Optical module makers and cloud/AI system builders; Lumentum does not name them. Two customers were 41.6% of last fiscal year's revenue (thesis file, from the 10-K). NVIDIA is an investor ($2.0bn convertible preferred, 10-K).
products.how_it_works: Lasers are grown and etched on indium phosphide wafers (AXT supplies substrates) in Lumentum's fabs, then placed inside transceivers that turn electrical signals into light pulses; in co-packaged optics an external high-power laser feeds optical engines next to the switch chip.
products.sales: Not disclosed by product. Proxy (labelled): total company revenue $1.01bn in Q4 FY2026; Q1 FY2027 guided to $1.225-1.275bn. Demand gap per the CEO on Bloomberg TV (secondary reports): about 70% of demand unmet for some products through 2027 and about 30% for others through 2028.
products.stage: Shipping in volume, capacity-constrained; added a fab in Greensboro, North Carolina; adding capacity at a second fab in Japan; new capacity about three years from decision to customer shipments (around 2029-2030).
products.size_for_company: Core of the business (inference, medium); the exact share of revenue was not checked this run.
products.competition: Peers named in this window's coverage: Coherent and Applied Optoelectronics. The CEO reportedly said Chinese transceiver makers supply about 70% of the US market (single tier-3 relay of Bloomberg TV; unverified).
products.why_investors_care: A longer shortage means pricing power and visible revenue; but growth is limited by how fast new capacity comes online, and long shortages push customers to qualify second suppliers.
products.watch_next: Q1 FY2027 call (2026-11-05): supply-vs-demand language, lead times, capital spending on the Japan fab, any long-term supply agreements or customer prepayments, gross margin.

products.name: Optical circuit switch (OCS)
products.what_it_is: A switch that redirects beams of light between fibres with tiny moving mirrors, without converting them to electricity.
products.analogy: A railway switch for light: trains change track without stopping at a station.
products.buyers: Hyperscale cloud operators; Lumentum's OCP talk on 2026-10-15 is co-presented with an architect from Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.
products.how_it_works: Mirrors steer incoming light to the chosen output fibre, letting operators re-wire large AI clusters in software with less power.
products.sales: 'Rapidly scaling past a $100 million quarterly revenue run rate' (management letter; run rate, not reported revenue). Not new this window.
products.size_for_company: About 8% of the Q1 FY2027 revenue guide midpoint ($1.25bn) if the run rate is $100m a quarter (arithmetic on management's wording).
products.why_investors_care: A second growth engine beyond lasers; management talks of 'revenue in the billions in upcoming years' (DEF 14A).
products.watch_next: OCP Global Summit talk 'Zero-Touch OCS Fabrics for AI Scale-Out Infrastructure at Hyperscale', Thursday 2026-10-15, 8:45-9:05 a.m. (San Jose).
